summary: Every company must keep a register of charges at its registered office to record all property and asset charges. A copy of the instrument creating the charge must also be kept there. Members and creditors can inspect these documents for free, while other people may have to pay a fee.
points: Companies must keep a register of charges at their registered office.
The register must include all charges and floating charges affecting any company property, assets, or undertakings.
A copy of the instrument creating the charge must be kept with the register.
Any member or creditor can inspect the register and instrument during business hours without paying any fees.
Any other person can also inspect them during business hours upon paying the required fees, subject to reasonable company rules.
example: Meera Textiles Private Limited recently took a bank loan and pledged its factory machinery as security. To follow the law, Meera Textiles Private Limited must now maintain a register of charges at its registered office, along with a copy of the document that created this charge. Rahul, a curious shareholder, visits the office during business hours and asks to see the register. The company must let Rahul inspect the register and document for free because he is a member. Later, a local business owner named Amit, who is neither a member nor a creditor, wants to look at the register. The company can allow Amit to inspect it during business hours, provided he pays the required fee and follows reasonable rules.

terms.meaning: An interest or lien created on the property or assets of a company as security for a loan or debt.
A type of charge on property or assets that changes from time to time in the ordinary course of business.
A formal legal document that creates or affects rights, such as the document creating a charge.
The official main address of a company where official records must be kept.

watch: People often confuse members and creditors, who get free inspection, with the general public, who may have to pay a fee.
